reason: The FLOPO bearer is pyrene. Its faces (ventral face, sides) can be flat.

'Optical quality' is too generic. The examples are colours (purple, reddish, dark), and some are about appendages, not the anther. A rule would map colour words to colour terms and leave this parent out.
Staminal appendages and staminodes can be fimbriate. The bearer is the stamen, which is acceptable.
Bract orientation (horizontal) is meaningful, and the examples fit.
Inflorescence bracts and floral scales have elliptic outlines.
'Delicate' and 'fragile' petals are a real texture, and the French 'délicats' and 'fragiles' agree.
Firm is a texture, and rhizomes can be firm.
Whole plants can be scaly throughout, as in ferns and bromeliads. Use the whole plant only when the text says 'throughout'.
Silky or sericeous hairs are common on phyllaries.
Wrong reading. 'Capillary' and 'fibriform' mean hair-thin, which is filiform. PATO fibrillary means made of fibrils.
Blotched leaves are common (red or purple blotches).
Hyaline margins are translucent, so transparent fits.
A pale achene is a colour state, and low saturation is a near match. Prefer a 'pale' colour value if one exists.
The abaxial epidermis can be rough, as in 'roughened abaxially'.
Phyllary shape is often triangular-lanceolate.
Filaments can be lanate or woolly.
Peduncles can be bristly.
The bearer is the floral corona. Its margins and lobes can be dentate. Some examples describe filament margins, which is acceptable for a corona.
Ovary cross-section can be circular, though a statement should say 'in cross section'.
Fronds can be entire (undivided), which is a normal fern character.
A corm can be globose or subglobose. The generic parent is acceptable, but a specific spheroid term is better when one exists.
Erose margins are common on bract margins.
A canaliculate (channeled) leaf apex or acumen is grooved.
A tessellate surface is a normal seed testa pattern.
Catkin width is a real dimension. The examples are 'length × width' pairs, so a size rule must split them.
Mericarp outline shape (ovate, elliptic) is meaningful. This is the generic 2-D shape parent.
Mericarps can be subglobose or globose.
A stigma can be quadrate or square.
Winged midribs are common, for example in ferns and mosses.
The bearer is the pinna. A pinna can be simple (undivided), which is the opposite of compound.
Pinnae and their stalks or rachises can be winged. The examples are partly about the rachis, so the bearer is only approximate.
Cone symmetry is meaningful, but only one flora supports it.
Wrong reading. 'Attenuated' here means gradually narrowed (a shape), but PATO 'reduced virulence' has 'attenuated' as a synonym for pathogens. Map it to the tapering or attenuate shape.
A blade can be variable (variant) in size or shape. This is common in floras.
Prickles can be broad, and broad-based prickles are common.
Weak prickles are a real description. This reads as strength or rigidity.
Nectary scales can be spatulate.
Anthers can be horseshoe-shaped, which is U-shaped.
'Present' is not a quality of the part. The examples say where rhizophores occur (position, distribution). Presence should be handled by a rule, and the position by a location pattern.
Perichaetial bracts are described as differentiated or not from vegetative leaves. This is a real moss character.
A pedicel can be simple (unbranched), but the examples are about trichomes and peduncles, which are other parts. A rule would need to tell trichome 'simple' from the bearer's own state.
'Short herbs' is plant height. A rule should map it to plant height (a height quality), not plain length.
Wrong reading. 'Leafy' means bearing leaves. PATO 'structure' is a generic relational attribute and does not say this.
Seeds can be crescent-shaped (lunate).
The bearer is the indusium. An indusium can be narrow.
Sori can be short.
The bearer is the pseudobulb. A pseudobulb can narrow toward its base or apex, which is tapered.
Stalks, stipes and stems can be thread-like.
Indusia can be elongate.
Wrong part. The examples describe the spur (of a flower), not a short shoot. A short shoot can spread, but these statements belong to the spur.
The bearer is the spathe. A spathe can be ovate or ovoid. This is the existing ovate-class reading.
Tepals can be small.
Wrong bearer. 'Capitula few' counts capitula inside a larger inflorescence, so the count belongs to the capitula (a counted part) and not to one capitulum.
The bearer is the disc gland. Disc glands can be erect.
The bearer is the tunic. A tunic apex or margin can be entire or not. Only one flora supports it, so check it.
A leaf apex can be truncate.
The bearer is the orchid labellum. A labellum can be striped, though 'banded' is a loose match for stripes.
The bearer is the stigma lobe. A stigma lobe can be oblong.
The bearer is the spathe. It can be glabrous or hairy, which is the pilosity attribute. Note that some examples describe other parts.
A palea can be longer than the lemma. This is a comparison, so a rule is needed to read the other part.
